cooling_items.text:
The building is not equipped with a centralized cooling system. Cooling within individual suites is provided by a combination of window-mounted air conditioners and portable indoor air-conditioning units.

These decentralized cooling devices are generally less efficient than modern centralized or heat-pump-based systems. Typical window and portable air-conditioning units operate with relatively low coefficients of performance (COP), often below 3.0, compared to high-efficiency heat pump systems which can achieve COP values exceeding 4.5–5.0 under favorable conditions.

In addition to reduced cooling efficiency, window-mounted air-conditioning units can negatively impact building envelope performance. Improper sealing around window installations may allow uncontrolled air infiltration during the heating season, increasing heat loss, draft complaints, and overall space-heating energy consumption. Installation of a air source heat pump (ASHP) system could be considered in a short term to mid term.
cooling_items.title: Window A/C Units

heating_items.text:
Space heating within individual suites is provided by in-suite electric resistance baseboard heaters, which operate independently in each unit and are controlled by local thermostats.

Electric resistance heating directly converts electrical energy into thermal energy and operates at an effective coefficient of performance (COP) of approximately 1.0. This means that one unit of electrical energy produces one unit of heat. While simple in design and relatively low in maintenance, electric baseboard systems are typically associated with higher operating costs compared to modern heat pump–based systems.

In comparison, high-efficiency air-source heat pump (ASHP) systems utilize a refrigeration cycle to transfer heat from the outdoor air into the building during the heating season. Modern ASHP systems can achieve seasonal heating COP values in the range of 3.0–4.0 or higher under favorable operating conditions. This represents a significant improvement in energy performance relative to electric resistance heating.

In addition to energy considerations, decentralized electric baseboard systems provide no cooling capability and offer limited opportunities for central monitoring or optimization. Temperature control and energy consumption vary between suites depending on occupant usage patterns. From a lifecycle perspective, while baseboard heaters have low mechanical complexity, the absence of centralized infrastructure limits system-level efficiency improvements.

Given the building’s age and the reliance on electric resistance heating, conversion to a heat pump–based system should be considered in the short to medium term as part of a broader modernization strategy aimed at improving energy efficiency, reducing operating costs, and providing integrated heating and cooling capability.
heating_items.title: Electric Baseboard Heater

measures.existing_conditions:
Windows and exterior doors located on the front façade of the building have been previously replaced and are in generally good condition. In contrast, the rear façade window and door assemblies remain original and were observed to be in poor condition.

The rear windows exhibit signs of frame deterioration, aging seals, and reduced air-tightness. Given the age of the assemblies, the insulating glazing units are likely operating below their original thermal performance due to seal
measures.measure_title: Replacement of Windows and Exterior Doors
measures.notes: Replacement of the original  windows and exterior doors
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended that the rear façade windows and exterior doors be replaced with modern high-performance assemblies. New glazing systems incorporating low-emissivity (low-E) coatings, thermally improved frames, and enhanced seal technology would reduce heat loss and improve overall building envelope performance.

Replacement exterior doors should include insulated cores, continuous weatherstripping, and improved air sealing to minimize infiltration.

Given that the front façade assemblies have already been upgraded, a phased approach targeting only the rear façade is appropriate and cost-effective. This targeted envelope improvement would enhance occupant comfort, reduce uncontrolled air leakage, and lower heating demand while aligning with long-term capital planning objectives.

measures.existing_conditions:
The building is currently served by a heating-only hydronic distribution system. Space heating is provided through copper-fin baseboard heaters and hydronic radiators supplied by a centralized boiler plant located in the main mechanical room.

The building does not have a central cooling system. No in-suite fan coil units, chillers, or centralized cooling infrastructure are present. As a result, suite-level cooling, where provided, relies on window A/C or portable air-conditioning units. These localized cooling devices typically operate independently, are relatively inefficient, and contribute to increased electrical demand during the cooling season.
measures.measure_title: Transition Baseboard Heater to Mini-Split Heat Pump Systems
measures.notes: Replace current system with air-source heat pumps, allowing simultaneous heating and cooling.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends replacing the existing hydronic baseboard heating systems with mini-split air-source heat pump (ASHP) systems to provide both space heating and cooling at the suite level.

The existing hydronic baseboard system relies on centrally generated hot water distributed throughout the building. While functional for heating, this system provides heating only, operates at relatively high distribution temperatures, and does not provide cooling. In addition, system efficiency is constrained by boiler plant performance, distribution losses, and limited zone-level control.

In contrast, mini-split heat pump systems typically operate at a COP of approximately 3 to 4 under suitable operating conditions, allowing them to deliver three to four units of heat for each unit of electrical energy consumed by transferring heat from the outdoor air to the indoor space. This results in a substantial reduction in energy consumption while maintaining or improving occupant comfort.

In addition to improved heating efficiency, the proposed mini-split systems would introduce dedicated cooling capability to the suites. This would eliminate the need for separate window-mounted or portable air-conditioning units, improving overall system efficiency, reducing peak electrical demand, and simplifying long-term maintenance.

The proposed upgrade would transition the building from an aging, single-function heating system to a modern, high-efficiency heating and cooling solution, improving occupant comfort, operational performance, and long-term energy efficiency.

*This measure is recommended subject to a detailed feasibility study to be carried out at the next project stage or as part of an ASHRAE Level 2 Energy Audit. The feasibility assessment should consider the available electrical service capacity, potential electrical infrastructure upgrades, and system integration constraints. It is also recommended that the existing hydronic heating system be retained as a backup system to ensure reliability and operational flexibility.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions: No anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve was observed downstream of the domestic hot water storage tank during the site visit.As a result, delivery temperatures are controlled locally or through fixed settings, increasing the risk of temperature fluctuation, scalding, and scale buildup within downstream piping and fixtures.
measures.notes: Install an anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve to improve DHW temperature control, enhance occupant safety, and reduce scaling-related maintenance.
measures.retrofit_conditions: Install an anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve on the domestic hot water system to maintain safe and stable delivery temperatures while protecting downstream piping and fixtures from scale buildup. This measure improves temperature control, reduces scald risk, and lowers long-term maintenance requirements by minimizing mineral scaling within the DHW system.

No widespread outages were observed during the walkthrough, and the overall lighting levels were appropriate for the building’s use. Further savings may be available through continued LED retrofit and the use of occupancy-based controls in selected low-traffic areas. Or installing light control in the parking area.
misc_items.title: Lighting condition and controls

misc_items.text: The building is equipped with double-pane windows with generally intact seals and caulking, providing effective air sealing and thermal performance. No significant air infiltration issues were observed during the site visit
misc_items.title: Window condition (good)

ventilation_items.text:
The building is equipped with a rooftop supply fan that provides ventilation air to the interior corridor spaces through centralized ductwork. Based on site observations, the unit appears to be original to the building (circa 1970) and shows visible signs of aging, including surface corrosion, weather-related deterioration, and general wear due to prolonged rooftop exposure.

No visible gas-fired heating section, cooling coil, or integrated conditioning components were observed during the assessment. As such, the system likely delivers unconditioned outdoor air to the corridors. Heating of common spaces rely on electric radiators.

Overall, the rooftop supply fan is considered to be in poor to fair condition due to age and exposure. While functional at the time of inspection, the equipment is approaching or exceeding its typical service life and should be evaluated for replacement in the short to medium term to ensure reliable ventilation performance.
ventilation_items.title: Very old supply fan/ventilation fan + poor condition + fan only

ventilation_items.text:
The building is equipped with a rooftop supply fan that provides ventilation air to the interior corridor spaces through centralized ductwork. Based on site observations, the unit appears to be original to the building (circa 1970) and shows visible signs of aging, including surface corrosion, weather-related deterioration, and general wear due to prolonged rooftop exposure.

No visible gas-fired heating section, cooling coil, or integrated conditioning components were observed during the assessment. As such, the system likely delivers unconditioned outdoor air to the corridors. Heating of common spaces rely on electric radiators.

Overall, the rooftop supply fan is considered to be in poor to fair condition due to age and exposure. While functional at the time of inspection, the equipment is approaching or exceeding its typical service life and should be evaluated for replacement in the short to medium term to ensure reliable ventilation performance.
